text.p: Australian pharmaceutical manufacturer F.H Faulding and Co Ltd said on Friday it remained on track for a stronger performance in 1996/97, subject to anticipated drug approvals in the United States.
"We are again very much dependent on new approvals and the introduction of new products in the U.S.," chief executive Ed Tweddel told Reuters.

"If they come through in the way we expect them to, yes we should be looking at a nice increase for the full year," he said, adding he did not expect there to be many surprises for the market in the company's half year results, due in March.
Faulding reported a net profit of A$28 million in the year to June 30, down from A$36.5 million a year earlier.
However, Tweddell said the Chinese market remained tough, particularly due to the Beijing government's austerity programme which impacted on reimbursement of drugs in hospitals.
"We are not going to have a good year in China ... I think it is going to be disappointing," he said.

Speaking at the opening of the company's A$10 million corporate headquarters' extension in Adelaide, Tweddell said Faulding had the possibility of some new approvals by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) soon.
The company currently has 14 products lodged with the FDA.
"That is what it is all about, keeping approval levels up by keeping submissions timely," he said.
Tweddell said there would be more acquisitions to follow the company's most recent purchase of the Irish pharmaceutical distributor Central Laboratories Ltd.
"We have said before we are looking to increase our critical mass in the U.S. and we have an expansion plan, always looking for ways of adding to our technology and skill levels," he said.
Faulding operates in the United States mainly through its subsidiary Faulding Inc.

Tweddell said Faulding strongly supported the Australian government's Factor F scheme, currently under review, which compensates drug companies for lower drug prices in Australia with payments for investment in research and development.

However, he said it had not budgeted for the scheme beyond 1997/98, having seen it as a launching pad for the competitive advantage needed to develop drugs like Kadian, an oral sustained release morphine product.

Of greater significance to Faulding's manufacturing operations in Australia, he said, was the government's approach to patents, particularly the issue of 'springboarding' for generics, allowing companies to develop a product before a patent expired.

"We need to have that springboarding provision ... otherwise we would have a competitive disadvantage and be forced to develop our products offshore," he said, adding he was confident the government would reach "the right position".
